chapter: Cecilia, Elvin Jones and jazz education
title: Teaching at Queens, Rutgers and Buffalo, and students like Najee
summary: He names students and colleagues, including the Jazz Professors and Lesotho tour, Nasar Abadey and Najee.

venues.name: State University of New York at Buffalo

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Before I stopped you to get specifics about those particular periods you were ­ -
Oh, I had mentioned that I taught a year at Queens College.

And as you go through talking about State University of Wisconsin or whatever, if there are particular aspects of those experiences, including students that you may have worked with or that are significant, we want that for the record.

Yeah. At Queens College there was a guy who came off and on and sat in with the band, but I guess he was too busy at that time, a trumpeter named -- his first name is Tom. Maybe you can enlighten me. I’ve forgotten his last name, but he went off into jazz fusion.
Tom Brown?
Tom Brown, right, yeah.
Funking in Jamaica I think was his big thing, on Arista.

Yeah, I wanted him to be there more often, but at that time he was just getting ready to get busy, so he couldn’t some around too much. At Davidson College of Rutgers University I was one of the jazz professors under Larry Ridley, with Ted Dunbar, Kenny Barron, and the late Freddie Waits. We had a quintet called the Jazz Professors. We went to Senegal -- not Senegal. Lesotho in southern Africa -- on a two-week educational tour and concert tour in which Dizzy Gillespie participated and the late Monk Montgomery as well. There were some students to come out of there that are fairly active on the musical scene. There was a guitarist, an exceptional guitarist named Josh Thompson. I don’t know if you ever heard of him. He’s into producing now. He’s just so broad-based, but he was a phenomenal guitarist and composer. From the Buffalo experience, SUNY at Buffalo, there was an alto saxophonist named Joe Ford that --
Joe was at Central State when I was at Antioch.
Oh, yeah.
He was in Wilberforce, Ohio. Wilberforce is like ten minutes from the other school systems where Antioch was, so I know Joe Ford from those days.
Yeah. All right, but Joe Ford actually wasn’t a student.
But he’s from Buffalo.
Yeah, so he was around, and then I got acquainted with him during that time.
Did you know a drummer up there named Nasar Abadey.
Yeah.
Well he’s here now.
He’s here? Yeah, right, that’s right.
That’s my instructor, my teacher.

Is that right? Yeah, I knew him well. In fact he went on a tour with me to -­ he went to Senegal with me as part of that Club Med thing. Or did I meet him -- I think I met him over there. He didn’t go with me. Someone else went with me, but I met him over there. We’ve played several times together. Nasar Abadey, yeah. So there have been some prominent students to come out of all these university settings in which I’ve taught, who are now professionals. Someone told me that Najee -- if you’re you hip to Najee?
Uh-huh.
-- was one of my students at one time.
One of the things, I’ve worked with Najee a lot, because he used to open for Freddie Jackson, and I would -- what’s the little diminutive singer who did the Whiz? The little, short -­
Oh, Stephanie Mills.

Stephanie Mills, and he opened for her. I would be a stage hand at those gigs. It became a little joke with us, because he would always quote -- in his performance he’d always drop in Confirmation, some bebop or hard bop little thing. It would be a

moment, and he segue into a spirituals thing, and then he’d go on to something pop, but he’d always dropped that somewhere in his performance, so I think -- I’ve always felt that he could play in a different context.
Yeah, he could have, I’m sure.
